nodes.description: The germline lesion is an unstable CTG-CAG repeat expansion on chromosome 13q21, in a region where ATXN8OS and the protein-coding ATXN8 overlap and are transcribed in opposite directions. The single expansion is therefore transcribed twice, in both senses, and everything downstream follows from that one fact: a CUG-repeat non-coding transcript from ATXN8OS and a CAG-repeat coding transcript from ATXN8. The repeat is highly unstable on transmission, tending to expand through the maternal line and contract through the paternal line, which is part of why the disease does not show the tidy repeat-size-to-onset relationship of the polyglutamine SCAs.
nodes.id: Bidirectional Transcription of the ATXN8OS/ATXN8 CTG-CAG Expansion

nodes.description: The non-coding CUG-expansion transcript accumulates as ribonuclear inclusions in the nuclei of selected neurons and glia, where it binds and sequesters MBNL1. This is the same class of RNA gain-of-function lesion that drives myotonic dystrophy type 1, arriving here through a repeat that is short by the standards of that disease. The genetic evidence is the strong part: removing Mbnl1 makes SCA8 mice worse, which is what a sequestration model predicts and a bystander model does not.

nodes.description: The convergence point. Purkinje cells are the sole output of the cerebellar cortex, and their firing is degraded here from two directions at once: loss of granular-layer inhibition from the RNA arm, and intranuclear polyglutamine inclusions from the protein arm. Progressive loss of cerebellar output produces the ataxia, the scanning dysarthria and the oculomotor signs, and the cell loss is visible on MRI as global cerebellar atrophy sparing the brainstem.
nodes.id: Cerebellar Purkinje and Deep Nuclear Circuit Dysfunction

nodes.description: With MBNL1 sequestered, the alternative splicing it normally regulates shifts across its CNS target set. This is the molecular consequence of sequestration and is separated from what any individual mis-spliced target then does, because the splicing shift is general while only one target has been traced through to a physiological effect.

nodes.description: The CAG-direction transcript is translated conventionally from an AUG start into a nearly pure polyglutamine tract, which forms 1C2-positive intranuclear inclusions in cerebellar Purkinje cells and brainstem neurons. This was discovered after SCA8 had already been characterised as a non-coding expansion disease, and it is why SCA8 is now described as involving toxic gain of function at both the protein and the RNA level rather than at one of them.

evidence.reference_title: Bidirectional expression of CUG and CAG expansion transcripts and intranuclear polyglutamine inclusions in spinocerebellar ataxia type 8.
evidence.snippet: the expression of noncoding (CUG)n expansion transcripts (ataxin 8 opposite strand, ATXN8OS) and the discovery of intranuclear polyglutamine inclusions suggests SCA8 pathogenesis involves toxic gain-of-function mechanisms at both the protein and RNA levels.

nodes.description: The defining feature. Gait instability is usually the presenting problem alongside dysarthria, and progression is slow enough to be measured in decades. Life span is typically not shortened, which is unusual among the dominant ataxias and shapes what management is for. Graded VERY_FREQUENT rather than OBLIGATE: non-ataxic presentations of a confirmed SCA8 expansion are documented, including dopamine-responsive parkinsonism, an ALS-like picture and isolated hemichorea, so the feature is not universal among affected carriers.

evidence.reference_title: Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 8.
evidence.snippet: SCA8 is a slowly progressive ataxia with onset typically in the third to fifth decade but with a range from before age one year to after age 60 years.

evidence.reference_title: Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 8.
evidence.snippet: Life span is typically not shortened.

nodes.description: The same expansion is translated from non-AUG start sites in more than one reading frame, producing homopolymeric proteins that no ordinary reading of the locus would predict: polyalanine, and later a polyserine product from the AGC frame. The polyserine burden increases with age and with disease severity. eIF3F was identified as a regulator of how much RAN protein accumulates, which is a rare handle on this class of mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 8 (SCA8) is caused by a bidirectionally transcribed CTG·CAG expansion that results in the in vivo accumulation of CUG RNA foci, an ATG-initiated polyGln and a polyAla protein expressed by repeat-associated non-ATG (RAN) translation.

nodes.description: The central experimental system for this disease. Because the transgene carries the whole locus under its own promoter, the model reproduces bidirectional transcription and therefore all three toxic species at once, which is what makes it usable for separating their contributions. The (CTG)116 versus (CTG)11 comparison is what establishes that the expansion itself is pathogenic rather than a linked marker. Nearly every interventional result this entry relies on - the Mbnl1 genetic interaction, the in vivo imaging of granular-layer inhibition, the polySerine white-matter pathology - comes from this model or its crosses.

evidence.reference_title: Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 8.

nodes.description: Upper motor neuron involvement is part of the recognised disease course. It is the phenotype the polySerine white-matter mechanism would predict, and one a purely cerebellar account does not.

nodes.description: For the scanning dysarthria, which is one of the two presenting features and a major determinant of employment and social participation.

nodes.description: The white matter regions carrying polySerine aggregates show demyelination and axonal degeneration, in human as well as mouse SCA8 brains. This is the part of the mechanism that reaches outside the cerebellar cortex, and the most plausible structural basis for the pyramidal signs and cognitive features a purely Purkinje-cell account leaves unexplained.
